neighbours.label: The source word cited in an etymology ('from the Latin sincerus'): a word mentioned as a word's origin, not the same word used normally
fire: The English word fragile comes from the Latin fragilis, meaning easily broken.
Etymology: from Old French corage, from Latin cor, meaning heart.
The verb to persuade derives from the Latin persuadere, to urge.
The adjective docile comes from the Latin docilis, easily taught.
From Middle English pardoun, from Old French pardon, from Latin perdonare.
The noun salary goes back to the Latin salarium, money for salt.
The word virtue comes from the Latin virtus, meaning manliness or worth.
The term democracy derives from the Greek demokratia, rule by the people.
quiet: The fragile vase came from a shop in Rome and was packed in paper.
Her courage came from her mother, who had raised four children alone.
He tried to persuade the board to approve the budget for next spring.
The docile horse walked behind the farmer all the way to the barn.
The judge granted a pardon to the old man after a long public campaign.
Her salary goes up every year, and she saves most of it for a house.
The word virtue appears often in his letters to the young prince.
The term of the mayor ended in May, and democracy in the town survived.
